title: World court to rule on Rohingya genocide case on 19 November
excerpt: The ICJ judgment in The Gambia v Myanmar is final. It will not change rations in Cox's Bazar, but it will shape the push for return and justice.
content:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver its judgment on Thursday, 19 November, in the case brought by The Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya, the court has announced. Court President Judge Iwasawa Yuji will read it at a public sitting at the Peace Palace in The Hague, according to Foley Hoag, the law firm representing The Gambia.

The case so far

  • Filed: November 2019, by The Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
  • January 2020: the court unanimously ordered Myanmar to take measures to protect the Rohingya still in the country.
  • July 2022: the court rejected all of Myanmar's objections to its jurisdiction.
  • January 2026: three weeks of hearings on the merits.

The case asks whether Myanmar as a state is responsible for genocide. It is not a criminal trial of individuals, Human Rights Watch (HRW) noted. The judgment is final and cannot be appealed. Myanmar denies the allegations and says its 2017 operation was a counter-terrorism campaign, bdnews24 reported. It will be only the third ICJ judgment in a genocide case.

"The International Court of Justice's Myanmar judgment will mark a crucial moment in the Rohingya's quest for justice," said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at HRW.

What it means for Bangladesh

More than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh from August 2017, and about 1.2 million now live in camps in Cox's Bazar and on Bhasan Char. A ruling against Myanmar would give Bangladesh stronger grounds to press for safe and voluntary return. It will not pay for the response: food rations were reduced in April and food aid is funded only to April 2027, as a New Age commentary also pointed out on 15 November.

Why it matters

NGOs working in the camps should expect strong interest from refugees, media and donors around the verdict, and possible protests or gatherings in the camps. Protection and community engagement teams may need to explain clearly what the ruling can and cannot change in daily life.

What to watch

The judgment on 19 November, Myanmar's response, and whether donors link new Rohingya funding pledges for 2027 to the outcome.
